entry: Phylum of mostly [[Flagellate|flagellate]] protists in the supergroup Discoba. Most species are unicellular and around 15–40 μm long, though some euglenids reach 500 μm. The phylum includes free-living species as well as parasites, some of which infect humans. Its four major groups are Kinetoplastea, Diplonemea, Euglenida and Symbiontida. Most species have two flagella. Many euglenids possess [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] and obtain energy through [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Reproduction occurs exclusively through cell division, during which the nuclear membrane stays intact during [[Mitosis|mitosis]]. The group is generally accepted as monophyletic and is probably part of the [[Excavata]], a grouping that has been challenged.

Topological invariant, a number describing the shape or structure of a [[Topological space|topological space]] regardless of how it is bent. Denoted χ, it was originally defined for polyhedra as V − E + F, where V, E and F are the numbers of vertices, edges and faces. [[Leonhard Euler]] introduced it for convex polyhedra but did not rigorously prove that it is an invariant. The surface of any convex polyhedron has χ = 2, as does the [[Sphere|sphere]]; toroidal polyhedra have χ = 0, like the [[Torus|torus]]. The concept was used to prove theorems about the [[Platonic solid|Platonic solids]]. In modern mathematics it arises from [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] and [[Homological algebra|homological algebra]].

Mathematical formula in [[Complex analysis|complex analysis]] linking the trigonometric functions with the complex exponential function. For any real number x, eⁱˣ = cos x + i sin x, where e is the base of the natural logarithm and i is the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]]. [[Leonhard Euler]] presented it in his 1748 treatise *Introductio in analysin infinitorum*. The formula remains valid when x is complex, and it is used throughout mathematics, physics, chemistry and engineering. Physicist [[Richard Feynman]] called it "our jewel" and "the most remarkable formula in mathematics". Setting x = π yields [[Euler's identity]].

Mathematical equation, eⁱπ + 1 = 0, linking five fundamental constants. It is a special case of [[Euler's formula]] evaluated at x = π. The constants are 0, 1, [[Pi|π]], [[E (mathematical constant)|e]] and the [[Imaginary unit|imaginary unit]] i. The equation also contains addition, multiplication and [[Exponentiation|exponentiation]] exactly once each. It is named after [[Leonhard Euler]] and is often cited as an example of mathematical beauty. A 1990 poll of readers by *The Mathematical Intelligencer* named it the "most beautiful theorem in mathematics". Mathematics writer Constance Reid called it "the most famous formula in all mathematics".

[[Castration|Castrated]] boy or man. The earliest records of intentional castration to produce eunuchs come from the [[Sumer|Sumerian]] city of Lagash in the 2nd millennium BC. Eunuchs were usually servants or slaves, castrated to make them less threatening at a royal court, where physical proximity to the ruler could bring great influence. They supposedly had no loyalties to the military, the aristocracy or a family of their own, and were therefore seen as more trustworthy. Eunuchs performed many functions, including courtier, espionage, guardian of harem servants, official and soldier. They often held significant power in the [[Byzantine Empire]], Imperial China, the [[Ottoman Empire]] and other cultures in Asia and Africa. Because their status was low, they could be replaced or killed without repercussion.

Mild or indirect word or expression substituted for one considered offensive or unpleasant. Euphemisms soften references to taboo or sensitive topics such as [[Death|death]], [[Disability|disability]], bodily functions, [[Pain|pain]] and violence, and are often used to soften [[Profanity|profanity]]. The term dates from the mid-17th century and derives from the Greek *euphēmismos*, meaning "use of words of good omen." Common strategies include understatement, metaphor and circumlocution, as in "passed away" for death. Linguist Steven Pinker described a "euphemism treadmill," in which neutral substitutes acquire negative connotations and must be replaced. Critics argue that in political and military contexts, euphemisms such as "enhanced interrogation" for [[Torture|torture]] or "collateral damage" for civilian casualties obscure causal realities and moral implications.

Large family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]], commonly called spurges or euphorbias. Most spurges are herbs, but some, especially in the tropics, are [[Shrub|shrubs]] or [[Tree|trees]]. *Hevea brasiliensis*, a tree native to the Amazon, supplies over 90% of global commercial rubber. The family is found worldwide, with its greatest diversity in the [[Tropics|tropics]] and species in nontropical areas of every continent except [[Antarctica]]. Many species have milky latex that can irritate the skin, and some are toxic. [[Cassava]] (*Manihot esculenta*) supports over 800 million people in tropical regions as a staple food. The ornamental [[Poinsettia]] (*Euphorbia pulcherrima*) is widely cultivated for holiday decoration, and *Ricinus communis* yields castor oil.

Longest river of [[West Asia|West Asia]]. Together with the [[Tigris]], it defined [[Mesopotamia]], "the land between the rivers." It rises in eastern Turkey, flows through Syria and Iraq, and joins the Tigris in the Shatt al-Arab, which empties into the [[Persian Gulf]]. Its drainage area of 440,000 sq km (170,000 sq mi) covers six countries. Irrigation from its waters supported early civilizations, including the Sumerians and Akkadians, through canal networks. Dams, including the Atatürk Dam in Turkey's Southeastern Anatolia Project, regulate flow for [[Hydropower|hydropower]] and irrigation but have reduced downstream volumes, adding to tensions over water allocation among Turkey, Syria and Iraq.

Largest continental area on Earth, comprising all of [[Europe|Europe]] and [[Asia|Asia]]. Some models treat it as a single physiographic continent, although the division into Europe and Asia is largely cultural and its borders have shifted over time. The European and Asian parts are conventionally separated by the [[Ural Mountains]], the [[Caspian Sea]] and the [[Caucasus Mountains]]. It covers about 55 million sq km, roughly 36 percent of Earth's land area, and is home to over 5.5 billion people. Eurasia connects to [[Africa]] at the [[Suez Canal]], and the two are sometimes combined as Afro-Eurasia, described as the largest contiguous landmass on Earth.

Grassland region of Eurasia, also called the Great Steppe. It stretches some 8,000 km (5,000 mi) westward from [[Manchuria]] across Mongolia, Xinjiang, Kazakhstan, Russia, Ukraine, Moldova, Romania and Hungary. Since the [[Paleolithic|Paleolithic]] age, the steppe has been the main overland route between Eastern Europe, North Asia, Central Asia and East Asia, a predecessor of the [[Silk Road]] and of the modern Eurasian Land Bridge. Its open terrain has been home to [[Nomad|nomadic]] empires and tribal confederations, including the Xiongnu, the [[Scythians]], Sogdia and the [[Mongol Empire]].

One of the largest living owl species, found across [[Eurasia]]. It has distinctive ear tufts, orange eyes and mottled, barred plumage. It is mostly nocturnal and hunts mainly small mammals such as [[Rodent|rodents]] and [[Rabbit|rabbits]], as well as birds and larger mammals. Its habitats include mountainous and rocky areas, woodland edges, coniferous forests and steppes. It nests on [[Cliff|cliff]] ledges, in gullies or among rocks, typically laying 2–4 eggs, and both adults provide care for the young for about five months. At least 12 subspecies have been described. The IUCN classifies it as least concern, although its population trend is decreasing.

[[Corvidae|Crow-family]] bird resident across northern [[Eurasia|Eurasia]]. Also called the common magpie, it is one of several magpie species in the crow family. In Europe, English speakers use "magpie" as a synonym for this species; the only other European magpie, the Iberian magpie, is restricted to the [[Iberian Peninsula]]. It is one of the most intelligent birds. The expansion of its nidopallium is roughly the same relative size as the brains of [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzees]], [[Gorilla|gorillas]], [[Orangutan|orangutans]] and [[Human|humans]]. It is one of the few bird species known to pass the mirror test. Its diet includes insects, fruit, seeds and carrion, and it caches food. It builds domed nests of sticks and mud and lays 5–7 pale blue eggs. It is classified as least concern by the IUCN.

Greek tragedian of [[Classical Athens|classical Athens]]. Along with [[Aeschylus]] and [[Sophocles]], he is one of the three authors of Greek tragedy whose names are attached to surviving plays. Ancient scholars attributed 95 plays to him, though the Suda says 92 at most. Nineteen attributed plays survive more or less complete, one of which, *Rhesus*, is often considered not genuinely his. More of his plays have survived intact than those of Aeschylus and Sophocles together. He is identified with theatrical innovations that present mythical heroes as ordinary people in extraordinary circumstances, and with a focus on his characters' inner lives. [[Aristotle]] called him "the most tragic of poets." The comedian [[Aristophanes]] lampooned his intellectualism, and his portrayal of women, especially in *Medea*, has drawn particular interest from modern scholars.

Top-tier men's professional [[Basketball|basketball]] club competition in [[Europe|Europe]]. Introduced in 1958 as the FIBA European Champions Cup, it was renamed the FIBA EuroLeague in 1996. Euroleague Basketball has organized it since the 2000–01 season. The league has 20 teams, 16 of them with long-term licences or wild cards. Real Madrid has won the most titles, 11, ahead of CSKA Moscow with 8. Its average league attendance of 10,383 in 2023–24 was the second-highest of any professional basketball league, behind the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]].

Currency of the eurozone, the official currency of 21 of the 27 member states of the [[European Union|European Union]]. Each euro is subdivided into 100 cents. The name was officially adopted in Madrid on December 16, 1995. The euro was introduced to financial markets as an accounting currency on January 1, 1999, replacing the European Currency Unit at a ratio of 1:1, and physical coins and notes entered circulation on January 1, 2002. It is the second-largest reserve currency and the second-most traded currency after the [[United States dollar|United States dollar]]. On July 13, 2022, it briefly reached parity with the dollar for the first time in nearly two decades.

Multinational twin-engine, supersonic, canard delta-wing multirole fighter. Designed originally as an air-superiority fighter, it is built by a consortium of [[Airbus|Airbus]], BAE Systems and Leonardo. Development began in 1983, but France left the collaboration over disagreements about design and operational requirements to develop the [[Dassault Rafale]] independently. The prototype first flew on March 27, 1994. The aircraft entered service in 2003 and made its combat debut in the 2011 military intervention in Libya. The procurement total stood at 769 aircraft as of June 30, 2026.

Pan-European television news network, headquartered in [[Lyon|Lyon]], France. Founded on January 1, 1993, it provides world news from a European perspective, streamed online, on [[YouTube|YouTube]] and on [[Mobile device|mobile devices]], and by satellite in Europe and North Africa. Alpac Capital, a Portuguese investment firm, is its majority owner. Its reliance on European Union grants has drawn scrutiny over its impartiality, while the network asserts editorial independence.

Smallest and least massive of the four [[Galilean moons|Galilean moons]] of [[Jupiter|Jupiter]]. It is an icy moon with a relatively young surface shaped by tidal heating, and it is probably the smoothest known solid object in the Solar System. A subsurface water ocean, kept liquid by tidal flexing, could harbor [[Extraterrestrial life|extraterrestrial life]]. [[Hubble Space Telescope|Hubble Space Telescope]] observations have suggested water vapor plumes. Simon Marius and [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo Galilei]] discovered the moon independently; Marius named it after Europa, the Phoenician mother of King Minos of [[Crete|Crete]] and lover of [[Zeus|Zeus]]. In 2022 the Juno spacecraft flew within about 320 km (200 miles) of it, and NASA's Europa Clipper launched on October 14, 2024.

Directly elected [[Legislature|legislative]] body of the [[European Union|European Union]]. Together with the Council of the European Union, it adopts EU legislation, normally following a proposal by the European Commission. It shares equal budgetary powers with the Council and can approve or reject the Commission, or force its resignation by censure. It has 720 members (MEPs) after the June 2024 elections and has been directly elected every five years since 1979. Its headquarters are in [[Strasbourg|Strasbourg]], France, while committee meetings take place mainly in [[Brussels|Brussels]], Belgium.

23-member international organization devoted to space exploration, headquartered in Paris. Founded in 1975 in the context of [[European integration|European integration]], it has a staff of around 3,000 and a 2026 annual budget of around €8.3 billion. Its human spaceflight programme includes the [[International Space Station|International Space Station]] and collaboration with [[NASA|NASA]] on the Artemis program, including manufacturing the European Service Module of the Orion spacecraft. ESA launches and operates uncrewed missions to the [[Moon|Moon]], [[Mars|Mars]], Jupiter, Venus, Mercury and the Sun, as well as to comets and asteroids. Europe's spaceport is the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou, [[French Guiana|French Guiana]]. Its Rosetta mission achieved the first landing on a comet in 2014.

Badger species of the family [[Mustelidae|Mustelidae]], native to Europe, West Asia and parts of Central Asia. Also called the Eurasian badger, it is classified as least concern on the IUCN Red List. Its weight ranges from 7–13 kg in spring to 15–17 kg in autumn. It is nocturnal and social, living in burrows called setts with multiple chambers and entrances. Their underground passages measure 35–81 m in length, and several families use a sett for decades. Although a [[Carnivora|carnivoran]], it is an omnivore that eats [[Earthworm|earthworms]], large insects, small mammals, carrion, cereals and tubers. Litters of up to five cubs are born in spring. Badgers can carry bovine [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]]; in England they are culled to reduce the disease in cattle, a practice whose efficacy is disputed and which some consider cruel.

Bison species native to Europe, the heaviest wild land animal on the continent. Also called the wisent, it is one of two living bison species, alongside the [[American bison|American bison]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] first described it scientifically in 1758. It was hunted to extinction in the wild in the early 20th century; the last wild animals of the Białowieża subspecies were shot in 1921, and the last Caucasian wisent in 1927. Captive animals were reintroduced into several European countries. The species was classified as endangered in 1996, later vulnerable, and is now near threatened. As of 2025, over 9,000 free-ranging individuals live in more than 40 herds, mainly in Poland, Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. It is not to be confused with the [[Aurochs|aurochs]], the extinct ancestor of domestic cattle.

Process of political, legal, social and economic integration among states in or near Europe. It has been pursued largely through the [[European Union|European Union]], though it also includes cultural assimilation. The [[Roman Empire|Roman]] consolidation of the continent set a precedent for unity, echoed by the [[Holy Roman Empire|Holy Roman Empire]], the [[Hanseatic League|Hanseatic League]] and the [[First French Empire|First French Empire]]. After World War II, the 1951 Treaty of Paris established the European Coal and Steel Community among six nations, the first transfer of national powers to a common institution. The 1992 Maastricht Treaty transformed the European Economic Community into the European Union. [[Winston Churchill|Winston Churchill]] called for a "United States of Europe" in 1946. Critics argue that supranational rulemaking dilutes national sovereignty and that unelected EU bodies have limited accountability, while supporters credit integration with curbing war between European states.

Small insectivorous [[Passerine|passerine]] bird of the [[Old World flycatcher|Old World flycatcher]] family Muscicapidae. Known in the British Isles as the robin or robin redbreast, it measures 12.5–14.0 cm (4.9–5.5 in) in length, with an orange-red breast and face, brown upperparts and a whitish belly. Males and females look alike; juveniles are freckled brown and lack the red breast. It ranges across Europe, as far east as [[Siberia|Western Siberia]] and south to North Africa. It is sedentary in the west and south of its range and migratory in the north and east, where winters are harsher. It forages mainly on the ground for invertebrates in the breeding season and takes seeds, berries and fruit in winter. Its population is stable, and the IUCN classifies it as least concern. In the British Isles it symbolizes Christmas.

Primarily ocean-going fish, one of six species in the temperate bass family Moronidae. It is native to the waters off Europe's western and southern coasts and Africa's northern coasts, and it also occurs in shallow coastal waters and river mouths. Also called branzino, it is commercially fished and raised, and is considered the most important fish cultured in the [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]]. In [[Ireland|Ireland]] and the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], the sea bass sold in restaurants is exclusively this species; in North America it is widely known as branzino. Adults usually weigh about 2.5 kg (5 lb 8 oz) and can reach 1 m (3 ft 3 in) and 12 kg (26 lb). Juveniles school and eat invertebrates, while adults are less social and mainly eat other fish, prawns and crabs. The IUCN lists it as Near Threatened because its population is decreasing.
